A landscape is everything you see when you look out across a wide stretch of land. Imagine standing on a hill and gazing into the distance. Everything in that view — the hills, the trees, the rivers, the fields, the sky touching the earth at the horizon — all of that together is a landscape. It is not just one thing you are looking at. It is the whole picture of a place.

1. A Natural or Physical Scene

This is the most common meaning. A landscape refers to the visible features of a large area of land, taken all together as one whole scene.

These features can include:

  • Landforms — mountains, valleys, hills, plains, cliffs
  • Water — rivers, lakes, ponds, wetlands
  • Plant life — forests, grasslands, deserts, farmlands
  • Human-made elements — roads, buildings, bridges, walls

The key point is that a landscape is not just one isolated feature. A single tree is not a landscape. A single mountain is not a landscape. But a valley with a winding river, surrounded by mountains and dotted with forests — that is a landscape. It is the combined, wide view of many features existing together in a space.

Examples:

  • "The landscape of Iceland is dramatic — black volcanic rock, green moss, glaciers, and geysers all visible at once."
  • "After the wildfire, the landscape looked bare and grey."
  • "Driving through the countryside, she admired the rolling landscape of farmland and hedgerows."

2. A Type of Painting, Photograph, or Artwork

In art, a landscape is a work — a painting, drawing, or photograph — whose main subject is natural outdoor scenery. Instead of painting a person (a portrait) or a bowl of fruit (a still life), the artist paints the land itself — mountains, meadows, skies, seashores.

Landscape painting has been one of the most important genres in art history. Artists like Claude Monet, J.M.W. Turner, and the Hudson River School painters in America dedicated much of their careers to landscapes.

Examples:

  • "The museum has a beautiful collection of 19th-century landscapes."
  • "She painted a landscape of the Scottish Highlands from a photograph she had taken."

3. The Character or "Feel" of a Particular Area

Sometimes, "landscape" refers not just to what you see, but to the distinctive character and quality of a place — the overall impression a region gives you. Two places can both have mountains, but their landscapes feel completely different.

Examples:

  • "The landscape of the Scottish Highlands has a wild, melancholy beauty."
  • "The flat, open landscape of the prairies can make a person feel very small."

Here, "landscape" captures something richer than a list of physical features — it conveys the mood and identity of a place.

4. Figurative Use — A Field, Situation, or Domain

This is a very widely used meaning in modern English. "Landscape" is often used figuratively (metaphorically) to describe the overall situation, state of affairs, or range of possibilities in any area of life — not necessarily a physical place at all.

Just as a physical landscape gives you the "big picture" of a place, a figurative landscape gives you the "big picture" of a situation.

Examples:

  • "The political landscape has changed significantly after the election." (= the overall political situation, the balance of power, who the key players are)
  • "We need to understand the competitive landscape before launching our product." (= who the competitors are, what the market looks like)
  • "The technological landscape of 2026 looks very different from 2010." (= the overall state of technology — what exists, what is dominant, what has changed)
  • "The cultural landscape of the city has shifted as new communities have moved in."

Any domain — business, politics, science, culture, education — can have its own "landscape." When someone uses the word this way, they mean: the full, wide picture of how things currently stand in that field.

5. Page or Screen Orientation

In computing, printing, and design, landscape refers to a horizontal page or screen orientation — one that is wider than it is tall. This is in contrast to portrait orientation, which is taller than it is wide.

The word is borrowed from the art world: a traditional landscape painting is typically wide and horizontal (to capture the broad expanse of land), while a portrait painting is tall and vertical (to capture a person standing upright).

Examples:

  • "Please print this spreadsheet in landscape mode so all the columns fit on one page."
  • "Rotate your phone to landscape for a better view of the video."
  • "The presentation slides are formatted in landscape orientation."

All the meanings of "landscape" share one unifying idea: a broad, wide view of something taken as a whole. Whether it is a physical scene, a painting, a political situation, or a page orientation, "landscape" always implies:

  • A wide scope — not just one small detail, but the bigger picture
  • Multiple elements existing together as a whole
  • A sense of surveying or taking in an entire scene at once

Since you want a complete understanding, it helps to know how "landscape" differs from words that seem similar:

  • Scenery — This is close to landscape, but scenery focuses more on the beauty of what you see, and it is often used for backgrounds in theatre or film. Scenery is more about the visual experience; landscape is more about the physical reality of the land itself.
  • View — A view is what you see from a specific point. A landscape is more about the land itself as a whole entity, regardless of who is looking at it or from where.
  • Terrain — Terrain is a more technical, military, or geographical word. It focuses on the physical shape of the land (is it flat? hilly? rocky?) without the visual or emotional richness that "landscape" carries.
  • Environment — Environment is broader and includes everything surrounding a living thing — air, water, climate, and more. A landscape is specifically the land as seen and experienced visually.

The word is flexible and powerful precisely because its core image — standing back and seeing the whole picture of something — applies equally well to a mountain valley and to a competitive business market. Once you understand that central idea, every use of the word will make immediate sense to you.
